atlasmind.ard.enabled.description: Enable Agentic Resource Discovery (ARD): the Resource Discovery tab in Settings, the /discover chat command, and the read-only discover-resources skill. Discovery only finds resources; it never installs anything without your action.
atlasmind.ard.enabled.markdownDescription:
Enable [Agentic Resource Discovery](https://github.com/ards-project/ard-spec) (ARD).

When on, AtlasMind exposes the **Resource Discovery** panel, the `/discover` chat command, and a read-only `discover-resources` skill agents can call mid-task. Discovery is **before invocation** — it only locates resources; nothing is installed without your explicit action, and Agent Finders ship disabled.

enumDescriptions: Ask each registry to merge results from upstream registries it knows about.
Follow referrals returned by a registry to other registries (depth-bounded).
Query only the selected registry; do not federate.
atlasmind.ard.federationMode.description: How ARD searches fan out across federated discovery registries.
atlasmind.ard.federationMode.markdownDescription:
How ARD searches fan out across federated discovery registries.

- `auto` — the registry merges upstream results server-side.
- `referrals` — AtlasMind follows referral records to other registries, up to a small depth bound (default).
- `none` — query only the selected registry.

Federation depth is capped to prevent referral loops, and all referral URLs are HTTPS-screened against private hosts.

atlasmind.ard.maxResults.description: Maximum number of results returned from an ARD discovery search.

atlasmind.ard.requestTimeoutMs.description: Timeout (in milliseconds) for each outbound ARD discovery request.

atlasmind.ard.allowInsecureEndpoints.description: Allow ARD Agent Finders that use http:// or localhost (e.g. the ARD conformance demo registry). When false, discovery requires HTTPS and rejects private/loopback addresses to prevent SSRF.
atlasmind.ard.allowInsecureEndpoints.markdownDescription:
Allow ARD Agent Finders that use `http://` or `localhost` — for example the [ARD conformance demo](https://github.com/ards-project/ard-spec) registry.

When `false` (default), discovery requires HTTPS and rejects private / loopback / link-local addresses to prevent SSRF. This setting only relaxes the check for finders **you** explicitly marked insecure; followed referral URLs are always screened.

atlasmind.chat.revealOnApprovalRequest.description: Bring the AtlasMind chat panel forward when a tool approval is waiting. A notification is shown either way — turning this off only stops the panel taking focus.
atlasmind.chat.revealOnApprovalRequest.markdownDescription:
Bring the AtlasMind chat panel forward when a tool approval needs an answer.

An approval **blocks the run until it is answered**, and the approval bar lives in this panel — which you may not be looking at. Without this, the run appears to hang.

A dismissible notification naming the waiting action is shown regardless, so turning this off only stops the panel taking focus; it never leaves you unaware. Nothing is announced while the panel is already on screen.

enumDescriptions: Not yet chosen — the setup guide will ask.
You run a Buzz relay on this machine (needs Docker).
Someone else runs the relay; you connect to their wss:// URL.
atlasmind.buzz.relayMode.description: Which way you run Buzz, so the setup guide shows only the path that applies. Set by answering the guide; it changes guidance only and connects nothing.

atlasmind.buzz.enabled.description: Enable Buzz (buzz.xyz) integration: record Buzz identities/channels on Project Director contacts and reach them via a Buzz deep link. Off by default; Buzz is an early-stage, self-hosted workspace and nothing connects to it until you opt in.
atlasmind.buzz.enabled.markdownDescription:
Enable [Buzz](https://buzz.xyz) integration — the open-source, Nostr-based workspace for humans and AI agents.

When on, Project Director contacts can carry a **Buzz** channel (npub / @handle / #channel) and AtlasMind can reach them via a Buzz deep link. Off by default: Buzz is early-stage and self-hosted, so nothing connects until you opt in. Automated outbound posting additionally requires a connected Buzz comms tool and the per-project `outboundEnabled` gate.

atlasmind.buzz.relayUrl.description: Buzz relay URL (BUZZ_RELAY_URL). Defaults to a local self-hosted relay (ws://localhost:3000). A remote relay sends project data off-machine and additionally requires atlasmind.buzz.allowRemoteRelay.
atlasmind.buzz.relayUrl.markdownDescription:
Buzz relay URL — the `BUZZ_RELAY_URL` a connected Buzz surface targets.

Defaults to a **local, self-hosted** relay (`ws://localhost:3000`), matching AtlasMind's local-first, self-sovereign posture. Pointing at a **remote** relay sends project data off-machine, so it is additionally gated behind `atlasmind.buzz.allowRemoteRelay` and the redaction/consent boundary.

atlasmind.buzz.inboundEnabled.description: Subscribe to Buzz activity and turn it into AtlasMind work items. Off by default; also requires atlasmind.buzz.enabled. The subscription is read-only — it can never post to Buzz.
atlasmind.buzz.inboundEnabled.markdownDescription:
Hold a **read-only** subscription to your Buzz relay and derive AtlasMind work items from the activity.

Off by default, and additionally requires `atlasmind.buzz.enabled` — nothing connects on upgrade. The subscription sends only subscribe/authenticate/keep-alive frames and **can never publish to Buzz**.

Conversations are **derived, never mirrored**: an inbound message becomes a follow-up with a pointer back to the Buzz thread, never the message body. Recording those follow-ups into project memory additionally requires `atlasmind.buzz.autoCreateFollowUps`.

An authenticating relay needs an agent key — run **AtlasMind: Set Buzz Agent Key**.

atlasmind.buzz.inboundChannels.description: Buzz channel ids (UUIDs) to subscribe to. Empty means every channel your agent key can read.
atlasmind.buzz.inboundChannels.markdownDescription:
Buzz **channel ids** (UUIDs) the inbound subscription should watch, scoping the subscription to just those channels.

Leave empty to receive activity from every channel your agent key can read. Get an id from `buzz channels list`.

atlasmind.buzz.autoCreateFollowUps.description: Record inbound Buzz activity as Project Director follow-ups. Off by default: project memory is git-tracked, so AtlasMind reports inbound items rather than writing them until you opt in.
atlasmind.buzz.autoCreateFollowUps.markdownDescription:
Record derived inbound Buzz activity as **Project Director follow-ups**.

Off by default, deliberately: `project_memory/` is **git-tracked**, so writing to it from a network event is something you should opt into rather than inherit from an upgrade. While off, inbound activity is reported without being persisted.

Only a short, sanitised title and a pointer back to the Buzz thread are ever stored — never the message body.

atlasmind.buzz.agentBindings.description: Map a Buzz identity (npub or 64-character hex) to an AtlasMind agent id, so inbound work from that Buzz agent lands with the right specialist.
atlasmind.buzz.agentBindings.markdownDescription:
Assign specific **AtlasMind agents** to specific **Buzz agents**.

Maps a Buzz identity to an AtlasMind agent id, so inbound work from that identity is attributed to the right specialist — a Buzz build-bot's messages can land with your DevOps agent instead of arriving unattributed.

```json
{
  "npub1abc…": "devops-engineer",
  "7e7e9c42…": "security-specialist"
}
```

Keys accept an `npub…` or a 64-character hex key (the bech32 checksum is validated, so a mistyped npub is rejected rather than binding to the wrong identity; an `nsec` secret key is refused). An unbound identity simply stays unassigned — AtlasMind never guesses an agent.

This is a **local routing preference only**. Buzz still owns the keypair, the directory, and the authorship ledger.

atlasmind.acp.hideConsoleWindows.description: Windows only: keep the complete ACP process tree behind one non-interactive, non-visible native supervisor so terminals cannot pop up or steal focus. Off by default.
atlasmind.acp.hideConsoleWindows.markdownDescription:
**Windows only, off by default.** Keep an ACP agent and every child process it launches behind one native supervisor. The parent creates a dedicated, non-interactive Windows window station/private desktop and one `SW_HIDE` console inherited by Node, native CLIs, and later shells. That prevents tool actions from allocating separate blank `conhost.exe` windows or taking keyboard focus. Windows npm adapters run under a real `node.exe`, not VS Code's GUI `Code.exe`.

With this unchecked, AtlasMind uses ordinary process launching. The first ACP start — and any restart after settings change or 30 minutes idle — may briefly show terminal windows created by the agent or its MCP servers. AtlasMind reuses a safe live session, so it no longer starts that process tree for every answer.

With this checked, AtlasMind uses a bundled, SHA-256-pinned native launcher. It passes through only stdin/stdout/stderr, starts the already-resolved agent command without a shell, and never switches to or remotely controls the private station. The VS Code status bar discloses a live private session without opening another native window. If the helper is missing, modified, blocked, or a real Node runtime is unavailable, the ACP launch fails visibly; AtlasMind does not silently fall back.

**Security software note:** unusual hidden UI boundaries and unsigned native helpers may be flagged or blocked by enterprise application control or EDR. The station's ACL comes from the current user's token and the child retains that user's filesystem/network authority: this is a window-placement control, not a sandbox. The hash pin checks AtlasMind's expected bytes; it is not an Authenticode signature. Leave this unchecked where policy forbids it, or if your security team has not approved the launcher.

atlasmind.acp.modelStanding.markdownDescription: Where each ACP model sits relative to its siblings, when AtlasMind cannot tell. The model *list* is always read from the agent itself — nothing is assumed about which models your plan has — but the wire format carries no capability field, so a model matching none of the built-in naming conventions is offered with **unknown** standing: fully routable, never preferred on capability, because a guessed ranking would misroute every turn without telling you. Declare it here to fix that, keyed on the model's display name or its wire value: `{ "Luna": "light", "Terra": "balanced", "Sol": "deep" }`. Values must be `light`, `balanced`, `deep` or `unknown`; anything else is ignored rather than guessed at.

atlasmind.acp.agents.description: ACP agents AtlasMind may use as subscription- or license-backed completion capacity. Empty by default — nothing is spawned until you name a command you have installed.
atlasmind.acp.agents.markdownDescription:
Agents AtlasMind can drive over the [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com) (ACP), using **your existing subscription or eligible product license** instead of pay-per-token API credit.

Each entry names a command **you have already installed**. AtlasMind never downloads or `npx`-fetches an agent behind your back, and the list is empty by default.

```json
[
  { "id": "claude",  "command": "claude-agent-acp" },
  { "id": "codex",   "command": "codex-acp" },
  { "id": "gemini",  "command": "gemini",  "args": ["--acp"] },
  { "id": "copilot", "command": "copilot", "args": ["--acp"] },
  { "id": "qwen",    "command": "qwen",    "args": ["--acp"] }
]
```

**Gemini eligibility:** `gemini --acp` requires an assigned Gemini Code Assist Standard or Enterprise license. Gemini Enterprise Standard and Plus include Code Assist Standard after separate assignment; Gemini Enterprise Business and Frontline do not include it, and personal Google AI Pro and Ultra plans and free individual accounts no longer authorize Gemini CLI. Those personal tiers stopped working with Gemini CLI on 18 June 2026; use AtlasMind's Google API provider for API-key access.

**`args` is not optional for the last three.** `gemini`, `copilot` and `qwen` are ordinary interactive CLIs until the ACP flag is passed — configure one without its flag and it opens a prompt that never answers.

These commands are transcribed from the [ACP registry](https://github.com/agentclientprotocol/registry). Others work too, including agents you install yourself: goose (`goose acp`), OpenCode (`opencode acp`), Cursor (`cursor-agent acp`), Kimi (`kimi acp`). Supply whatever command starts the agent in ACP mode.

By default agents run as a **completion source, not an executor**: no MCP servers are passed through and every permission request they make is refused. Set `#atlasmind.acp.toolsEnabled#` to make tool-backed ACP turns eligible and automatically allow their operations without another prompt. AtlasMind still logs every request and answers only `allow_once` on the wire.

Signing in is always the agent's own login flow — AtlasMind never handles that credential. Compared with the argv-based CLI bridge it replaced, this streams, has no ~26,000-character prompt ceiling, and can send images when the agent declares support.

atlasmind.buzz.autonomousReplies.description: ⚠️ Not yet active — this setting is declared but nothing reads it, so changing it currently has no effect. When wired, it will let AtlasMind agents reply to Buzz identities you have bound to an agent without confirming each message. Until then every Buzz send still asks for confirmation — the safe direction, but not what this switch implies.
atlasmind.buzz.autonomousReplies.markdownDescription:
**Not yet active.** This setting is declared but nothing reads it, so changing it has no effect today: every Buzz send still asks for confirmation.

When it is wired it will allow **agent-to-agent** Buzz replies to go out without a dialog, so an AtlasMind specialist can hold a loop with a Buzz agent. The design is deliberately narrow:

- It will apply **only** to recipients listed in `atlasmind.buzz.agentBindings`. That binding is your declaration that the identity is an agent — AtlasMind never infers it, and an unbound identity is treated as a person who may act on what it reads.
- It will be **rate-bounded** per recipient by `atlasmind.buzz.autonomousReplyLimitPerHour`. A loop that re-fires on every inbound event is the realistic failure, and there is no unsend.
- Inbound Buzz messages are **untrusted input**. An agent that reads a message and replies autonomously gives its author partial influence over what AtlasMind then says to others. Arm this only where that is acceptable.

atlasmind.buzz.autonomousReplyLimitPerHo.description: ⚠️ Not yet active — this setting is declared but nothing reads it, so changing it currently has no effect. When autonomous replies are wired, this will cap them per recipient per hour; once reached, the next message needs confirmation.
atlasmind.buzz.autonomousReplyLimitPerHo.markdownDescription:
Cap on autonomous replies **per recipient per hour** when `atlasmind.buzz.autonomousReplies` is on.

When the cap is reached the next message falls back to a confirmation dialog rather than being dropped, so a stuck loop becomes visible instead of silent.

atlasmind.buzz.allowRemoteRelay.description: Allow a non-local Buzz relay URL. When false (default), only loopback/localhost relays are used so project data stays on-machine.
atlasmind.buzz.allowRemoteRelay.markdownDescription:
Allow `atlasmind.buzz.relayUrl` to point at a **non-local** (remote) Buzz relay.

When `false` (default), only a loopback/localhost relay is used so project data stays on-machine. Set to `true` only when you intend to send project communications to a remote Buzz workspace, and expect the same redaction/consent boundary AtlasMind applies to any off-machine send.

atlasmind.presence.keepAwake.description: Keep this computer awake (prevent system sleep) while an AtlasMind activity needs the agent to stay online — a long Mission Loop run, an active Remote Control gateway session, or a connected Buzz presence. Off by default: AtlasMind never holds your machine awake unless you opt in, and the wake lock is released the moment the activity ends.
atlasmind.presence.keepAwake.markdownDescription:
Keep this computer awake — prevent the OS from sleeping — **while an AtlasMind activity needs the agent to stay online**: a long autonomous **Mission Loop** run, an active **Remote Control** gateway session, or a connected **Buzz** presence.

When `false` (default), AtlasMind never holds a wake lock; your normal power settings apply and a background run may be suspended when the machine sleeps. When `true`, AtlasMind acquires an OS keep-awake lock (Windows `SetThreadExecutionState`, macOS `caffeinate`, Linux `systemd-inhibit`) and releases it as soon as it is no longer needed.

This affects power use. It is additionally constrained by `atlasmind.presence.acPowerOnly` (suspended on battery by default) and auto-released by `atlasmind.presence.maxAwakeMinutes`. The status bar shows when the machine is being held awake; click it to stop.

atlasmind.presence.keepDisplayAwake.description: When keep-awake is active, also keep the display on. Off by default: AtlasMind keeps the system awake but lets the screen sleep, which uses less power. Only enable if an activity needs the display on.
atlasmind.presence.keepDisplayAwake.markdownDescription:
When `atlasmind.presence.keepAwake` is holding the system awake, **also keep the display powered on**.

When `false` (default), AtlasMind keeps the *system* from sleeping so the agent stays online, but still lets the **screen** turn off — the lower-power option that is enough for headless runs, remote sessions, and Buzz presence. Set to `true` only when an activity genuinely needs the display awake. Has no effect unless `keepAwake` is `true`. (On Linux the system inhibitor already keeps the machine working; display behaviour follows your desktop settings.)

atlasmind.presence.acPowerOnly.description: Only keep the computer awake while it is on AC (mains) power. When true (default), keep-awake is automatically suspended on battery so AtlasMind never drains an unplugged laptop; it resumes when you reconnect power.
atlasmind.presence.acPowerOnly.markdownDescription:
Only hold the keep-awake lock while the computer is running on **AC (mains) power**.

When `true` (default, safest), `atlasmind.presence.keepAwake` is **automatically suspended on battery** so AtlasMind never keeps an unplugged laptop from sleeping and draining its battery; the lock is re-acquired when you reconnect power. Set to `false` only if you deliberately want a run to hold the machine awake on battery. Has no effect unless `keepAwake` is `true`.

atlasmind.presence.maxAwakeMinutes.description: Safety backstop: automatically release the keep-awake lock after this many minutes, even if an activity is still running (0 = no backstop; hold until the activity ends). Prevents a stuck activity from holding the machine awake indefinitely.
atlasmind.presence.maxAwakeMinutes.markdownDescription:
Safety backstop: automatically **release** the keep-awake lock after this many minutes, even if a qualifying activity is still running.

This bounds the maximum time AtlasMind can hold your machine awake, so a stuck or runaway activity can never keep it awake indefinitely. When the backstop fires, the activity keeps running under your normal power settings (and may be suspended if the machine then sleeps).

Examples:
- Default balance: `240` (4 hours)
- Short supervised sessions: `60`
- No backstop — hold until the activity ends: `0`

Has no effect unless `atlasmind.presence.keepAwake` is `true`.

enumDescriptions: Never automatically update agent definitions.
Update the agent definition every time the agent is used.
Update the agent definition if it has not been refreshed in the last 24 hours.
Update the agent definition if it has not been refreshed in the last 7 days.
Update the agent definition if it has not been refreshed in the last 30 days.
atlasmind.agentAutoUpdateCadence.description: How often AtlasMind uses AI to automatically refresh user-defined agent system prompts and descriptions, keeping them modern, accurate, and legally compliant.
atlasmind.agentAutoUpdateCadence.markdownDescription:
How often AtlasMind automatically refreshes user-defined agent definitions using AI. When a refresh is due, the agent's system prompt and description are reviewed and updated to reflect current best practices, remove outdated instructions, and ensure legal compliance across major territories (US, EU, UK, Canada, Australia). The check happens on the next use of that agent.

Built-in agents are never auto-updated. Individual agents can opt out via the **Exclude from auto-updates** checkbox in the Agent Manager.

Examples:
- Set-and-forget personal agents: `monthly`
- Team agents that evolve with your stack: `weekly`
- Always-current agents for regulated industries: `daily`
- Default (no automatic updates): `never`

atlasmind.budgetMode.markdownDescription:
Budget preference for model selection.

Use `cheap` to keep routing on the lowest-cost acceptable models, `balanced` for the default mix, `expensive` to unlock premium reasoning models, or `auto` to let AtlasMind infer the tier from the task.

Examples:
- Solo scratchpad or note-heavy work: `cheap`
- Day-to-day engineering work: `balanced`
- Architecture reviews, migrations, or ambiguous debugging: `expensive`
- Shared team workspace with mixed task sizes: `auto`

atlasmind.speedMode.markdownDescription:
Speed preference for model selection.

Use `fast` to bias toward quick-response models, `balanced` for a normal tradeoff, `considered` to allow slower reasoning-heavy models, or `auto` to let AtlasMind choose based on task complexity.

Examples:
- Tight feedback loops while editing: `fast`
- General coding and chat: `balanced`
- Root-cause analysis or long-form planning: `considered`
- Teams switching between support, coding, and review: `auto`

atlasmind.feedbackRoutingWeight.description: How strongly saved thumbs-up or thumbs-down feedback should influence future model routing. Set to 0 to disable the feedback bias.
atlasmind.feedbackRoutingWeight.markdownDescription:
How strongly saved thumbs-up or thumbs-down feedback should influence future model routing. AtlasMind still caps the effect so votes cannot override capability, budget, speed, or provider-health gates.

Examples:
- Disable feedback-weighted routing: `0`
- Default slight bias: `1`
- Stronger but still bounded nudge: `1.5`

Use this when you want feedback to matter more or less without deleting the recorded vote history.

atlasmind.planningModelId.description: Optional model ID to pin for the planning/decomposition phase (the 'brain'). Leave empty to route planning normally.
atlasmind.planningModelId.markdownDescription:
Optional model ID pinned for the planning/decomposition phase — the project planner's 'brain'. Planning is a no-tool reasoning step, so this is a good place to use a strong reasoner (or a Claude subscription via `acp`) while execution subtasks still route to tool-capable workers.

When set to a known model ID, the planner uses it directly (bypassing budget/speed gates, since it is a deliberate choice); execution routing is unaffected. Leave empty (default) to route planning with normal budget/speed/outcome scoring. If the model is unknown or unavailable, AtlasMind falls back to normal routing.

Examples:
- `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4`
- `acp/claude@opus`
- `openai/o3`

atlasmind.synthesisModelId.description: Optional model ID to pin for the synthesis phase (summarizing results/sessions into reasoning context). Leave empty to route synthesis normally.
atlasmind.synthesisModelId.markdownDescription:
Optional model ID pinned for the synthesis phase — summarizing results or a chat session into reusable reasoning context. Like planning, synthesis is a no-tool reasoning step, so this completes the planner-brain / tool-executor / synthesis role-routing trio: pin a strong reasoner here while tool-using execution still routes to workers.

When set to a known model ID, synthesis uses it directly (bypassing budget/speed gates); empty (default) routes synthesis with normal scoring. Falls back to normal routing if the model is unknown.

Examples:
- `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4`
- `acp/claude@opus`

atlasmind.draftModelId.description: Optional model ID pinned to draft mechanical/low-stakes tasks (e.g. a fast local model). Struggle-gated escalation upgrades to a stronger model if the draft falls short. Leave empty to route normally.
atlasmind.draftModelId.markdownDescription:
Optional model ID pinned to **draft** mechanical, low-stakes tasks (routine edits, script runs, narrow test generation) — the local-draft half of local-draft / frontier-escalate routing. A fast local model is a good choice.

When set, draftable tasks (auto budget + mechanical) start with this model; if the draft struggles (low confidence / repeated tool failures), AtlasMind's existing escalation upgrades to a stronger reasoning-capable model automatically. The pin applies only to the first attempt and never blocks escalation. Empty (default) routes normally; an unknown model falls back to normal routing.

Examples:
- `local/llama-3.1-8b-instruct`
- `google/gemini-2.0-flash`

id.description: Stable identifier used to attribute routed local models to this endpoint. Auto-generated from the label when omitted.

label.description: Human-facing name shown in provider surfaces (e.g. "Ollama", "LM Studio"). Inferred from the base URL when omitted.

baseUrl.description: OpenAI-compatible base URL for this local engine, e.g. http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1.

atlasmind.localOpenAiEndpoints.description: Labeled local OpenAI-compatible endpoints AtlasMind aggregates under the Local provider. Each entry has a stable id, a human-facing label, and a baseUrl.
atlasmind.localOpenAiEndpoints.markdownDescription:
Configure one or more labeled local OpenAI-compatible endpoints AtlasMind aggregates under the **Local** provider. Each entry has a stable `id`, a human-facing `label`, and a `baseUrl`, which lets AtlasMind keep multiple local engines online together and still show which endpoint owns each routed local model.

Manage these from **AtlasMind Settings → Models & Integrations → OpenAI-compatible endpoints** rather than editing JSON by hand.

Example:
```json
[
  { "id": "ollama", "label": "Ollama", "baseUrl": "http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1" },
  { "id": "lm-studio", "label": "LM Studio", "baseUrl": "http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1" }
]
```

When only the legacy `atlasmind.localOpenAiBaseUrl` is explicitly set, AtlasMind auto-migrates it into this structured list once.

atlasmind.localGpu.enabled.description: Admit local model requests against a VRAM budget so two runtimes on one graphics card cannot over-commit it.
atlasmind.localGpu.enabled.markdownDescription:
Admit local model requests against a VRAM budget.

AtlasMind can issue local calls from several places at once — the subtask scheduler, project bootstrap, background maintenance — and Ollama and LM Studio each decide what fits without knowing the other exists. When on, AtlasMind measures free VRAM, queues requests that will not fit, and fails over to another provider rather than over-committing the card.

Turn this off to restore the previous behaviour, where every local request was sent immediately.

atlasmind.localGpu.maxConcurrentRequests.description: Concurrent local model requests allowed regardless of available VRAM.
atlasmind.localGpu.maxConcurrentRequests.markdownDescription:
Concurrent local model requests allowed regardless of available VRAM.

Requests against a model *already loaded* cost only their own context cache, so a burst against one model is cheap and mostly runs in parallel. Requests needing *different* models are serialised by the VRAM budget whatever this is set to.

This is also the only control that applies when free VRAM cannot be measured (AMD, Intel, Apple Silicon, or no `nvidia-smi`).

atlasmind.localGpu.safetyMarginMb.description: Megabytes of free VRAM left unclaimed, so a model loading cannot squeeze the desktop.
atlasmind.localGpu.safetyMarginMb.markdownDescription:
Megabytes of free VRAM left unclaimed.

Subtracted from the free memory the driver reports. This is the limb that normally decides, and it covers what your desktop will allocate *while* a model is loading — opening a browser tab mid-load is ordinary.

Because free memory is measured rather than assumed, this does not need to account for what Windows and your applications are already using: that is already excluded.

atlasmind.localGpu.reserveMb.description: Megabytes of the card AtlasMind will never occupy, as a ceiling on its own share.
atlasmind.localGpu.reserveMb.markdownDescription:
Megabytes of the card AtlasMind will never occupy.

**This is a ceiling on AtlasMind's own share, not a reserve for your operating system.** Your desktop is protected by measuring free VRAM, which already accounts for it.

This limb answers a different question: *has AtlasMind taken more of the card than you want it to?* It keeps applying as AtlasMind's own footprint grows, so raising it caps how much of the card AtlasMind will hold at once. Set to `0` to let the free-memory measurement govern alone.

atlasmind.localGpu.maxResidentModelsWhen.description: Models AtlasMind may keep loaded per runtime when free VRAM cannot be measured.
atlasmind.localGpu.maxResidentModelsWhen.markdownDescription:
Models AtlasMind may keep loaded per runtime when free VRAM cannot be measured.

Applies on AMD, Intel and Apple Silicon, or anywhere `nvidia-smi` is unavailable. Limiting how many *distinct* models stay loaded is the only bound available without a memory reading — limiting concurrent requests would not help, because Ollama keeps a model in memory for minutes after a request finishes.

Raise it if you have plenty of unified memory.

atlasmind.localGpu.evictOwnModels.description: Let AtlasMind unload models it loaded itself to make room for another. Models you loaded by hand are never unloaded.
atlasmind.localGpu.evictOwnModels.markdownDescription:
Let AtlasMind unload models **it loaded itself** to make room for another.

A model you loaded by hand — in the LM Studio app, or with `ollama run` — is never unloaded, whatever the pressure. AtlasMind tracks which models it caused to load and only ever releases those.

A model is only released when it has no request in flight and has been idle for a moment, and only when releasing it would actually free enough room; unloading something and still not fitting would cost the reload for nothing.

Turn this off to leave every loaded model alone and simply wait for room.

atlasmind.localOpenAiBaseUrl.description: Base URL for a local OpenAI-compatible model endpoint such as Ollama or LM Studio.
atlasmind.localOpenAiBaseUrl.markdownDescription:
Base URL for a local OpenAI-compatible model endpoint such as Ollama or LM Studio. AtlasMind appends the provider-specific chat paths under this base URL.

Examples:
- Ollama default: `http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1`
- LM Studio local server: `http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1`
- Remote self-hosted gateway on a lab network: `http://10.0.0.25:8080/v1`

For team or scaled deployments, point this at a stable gateway or reverse proxy rather than an individual developer machine.

atlasmind.azureOpenAiEndpoint.description: Azure OpenAI resource endpoint used for deployment-based chat routing, for example https://your-resource.openai.azure.com.
atlasmind.azureOpenAiEndpoint.markdownDescription:
Azure OpenAI resource endpoint used for deployment-based chat routing. This should be the resource endpoint, not a deployment or API path.

Example:
- `https://your-resource.openai.azure.com`

In larger environments, keep this aligned with the approved regional Azure OpenAI resource for your team, then manage access with SecretStorage-backed API keys and deployment allow-lists.

atlasmind.azureOpenAiDeployments.description: Azure OpenAI deployment names that AtlasMind should surface as routed models.
atlasmind.azureOpenAiDeployments.markdownDescription:
Azure OpenAI deployment names that AtlasMind should surface as routed models. Use deployment names exactly as they exist in Azure.

Examples:
- Single deployment: `["gpt-4.1"]`
- Split by workload: `["gpt-4.1-mini", "gpt-4.1", "o4-mini"]`
- Enterprise setup with separate safety-reviewed deployments per capability: `["chat-standard", "reasoning-premium", "vision-approved"]`

Keep this list intentionally small so only approved deployments appear in routing.

atlasmind.bedrock.region.description: AWS region used for Amazon Bedrock model invocations, for example us-east-1.
atlasmind.bedrock.region.markdownDescription:
AWS region used for Amazon Bedrock model invocations. AtlasMind signs requests for the region you specify here.

Examples:
- `us-east-1` for common Bedrock availability
- `us-west-2` for teams standardizing on West US adjacency

In multi-account or compliance-sensitive setups, choose the region that matches your approved Bedrock access boundary and the models listed in `atlasmind.bedrock.modelIds`.

atlasmind.bedrock.modelIds.description: Amazon Bedrock model IDs AtlasMind should expose as routed models, such as anthropic.claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219-v1:0.
atlasmind.bedrock.modelIds.markdownDescription:
Amazon Bedrock model IDs AtlasMind should expose as routed models. Use the full Bedrock model ID, not a friendly alias.

Examples:
- `["anthropic.claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219-v1:0"]`
- `["anthropic.claude-3-5-haiku-20241022-v1:0", "amazon.nova-pro-v1:0"]`

For larger organizations, use this as an allow-list so AtlasMind only routes to approved Bedrock models.

atlasmind.ssotPath.description: Relative path to the SSOT memory folder. If that path is missing, AtlasMind auto-detects an existing MindAtlas project in the current workspace when possible.
atlasmind.ssotPath.markdownDescription:
Relative path to the SSOT memory folder. AtlasMind expects a safe workspace-relative path and will auto-detect an existing memory folder when possible if the configured path is missing.

Examples:
- Default project memory: `project_memory`
- Monorepo app memory: `apps/api/project_memory`
- Team convention with shared docs folder: `docs/atlasmind-memory`

Prefer stable relative paths so onboarding, imports, and automation all resolve the same folder structure.

atlasmind.autoRefreshStaleMemory.description: Automatically re-import stale imported SSOT memory entries on startup and file changes. Off by default — the re-import is an expensive LLM re-summarization; when off, AtlasMind still flags stale memory so you can refresh on demand via Update Memory.
atlasmind.autoRefreshStaleMemory.markdownDescription:
Automatically re-import stale imported SSOT memory entries on startup and when workspace files change.

**Off by default.** The auto-refresh re-summarizes every stale imported entry with the LLM, which is slow on startup and costs tokens. When off, AtlasMind still detects staleness and surfaces the **Update Memory** action so you can refresh on demand. Turn this on only if you want imported memory kept continuously in sync automatically and accept the cost.

Examples:
- Fast startup, refresh memory manually: `false` (default)
- Always keep imported memory in lockstep with the workspace: `true`

atlasmind.autoStartProposedProjectRuns.description: Allow proposed project runs to start automatically only while Autopilot is on. Interactive chat instead shows Start run, Save for later, and Cancel actions. The file-count safety gate still applies.
atlasmind.autoStartProposedProjectRuns.markdownDescription:
Controls whether a project-run proposal may flow straight into execution while **Autopilot is ON**.

Behaviour:
- **Autopilot ON + setting ON** — the run starts immediately with a brief notice.
- **Autopilot OFF** — chat shows a decision card with **Start run**, **Save for later**, and **Cancel**.
- **Setting OFF** — the decision card is shown even under Autopilot.
- **Save for later** creates a reviewed preview in Project Run Center without executing it.
- Unusually large runs still hit the `projectApprovalFileThreshold` safety gate before changing files.

Examples:
- Permit hands-off proposal flow only under Autopilot: `true` (default)
- Always require a run decision card: `false`

atlasmind.showImportProjectAction.description: Show the Import Existing Project toolbar action in the AtlasMind Memory view.
atlasmind.showImportProjectAction.markdownDescription:
Show the Import Existing Project toolbar action in the AtlasMind Memory view. Disable this if you want a cleaner sidebar for already-bootstrapped repositories.

Examples:
- Personal workspace still onboarding projects: `true`
- Locked-down team workspace with a standardized import flow handled elsewhere: `false`

atlasmind.toolApprovalMode.description: How AtlasMind requests approval before running tools with side effects or external execution. Each mode is described by what it does NOT prompt for. The last two are different axes, not a stricter and a looser setting: ask-on-external gates anything leaving the editor but allows local file writes, while allow-safe-readonly does the opposite.
atlasmind.toolApprovalMode.markdownDescription:
How AtlasMind requests approval before running tools with side effects or external execution. This is the main safety dial for automation.

**Each mode is described by what it lets through without asking** — that is the part you need to know, and naming only the additions is how a mode came to be chosen for the wrong reason.

- `always-ask`: nothing. Every tool action prompts.
- `ask-on-write`: reads — local reads, git reads, and remote reads that change nothing.
- `ask-on-external`: everything local, **including file writes, deletes and commits**. It prompts for anything that leaves the editor: terminal, network, audio.
- `allow-safe-readonly`: local reads, git reads and terminal reads. Writes and external calls prompt.

**The last two are different axes, not a stricter and a looser setting.** `ask-on-external` asks *did this leave the machine?*; `allow-safe-readonly` asks *did this change something?* Neither gates a superset of the other, so moving between them tightens one thing and loosens another.

Examples:
- Highly regulated repo: `always-ask`
- Normal coding workflow: `ask-on-write`
- Trusted local automation where the risk you care about is reaching outside: `ask-on-external`
- Read-only investigation or audits: `allow-safe-readonly`

atlasmind.allowTerminalWrite.description: Allow write-capable terminal subprocesses such as installs and commits after explicit approval.
atlasmind.allowTerminalWrite.markdownDescription:
Allow write-capable terminal subprocesses such as installs and commits after explicit approval. This controls whether AtlasMind may use terminal-based commands that can mutate the workspace or repository.

Examples:
- Investigation-only mode: `false`
- Developer sandbox where installs and generators are expected: `true`

Keep this off in repositories where package installation, generated files, or git history changes must go through separate review controls.

atlasmind.autoVerifyAfterWrite.description: Run configured verification scripts after successful workspace write tools such as file-edit, file-write, and git-apply-patch.
atlasmind.autoVerifyAfterWrite.markdownDescription:
Run configured verification scripts after successful workspace write tools such as file-edit, file-write, and git-apply-patch. This helps catch regressions immediately after AtlasMind changes files.

Examples:
- Tight local loop: `true` with `autoVerifyScripts` set to `["test"]`
- Large monorepo where verification is handled elsewhere: `false`
- CI-like local enforcement: `true` with multiple scripts such as `test`, `lint`, and `typecheck`

atlasmind.autoVerifyScripts.description: Package scripts to run after successful write operations. Script names are sanitized and invoked without shell interpolation.
atlasmind.autoVerifyScripts.markdownDescription:
Package scripts to run after successful write operations. AtlasMind runs these as package scripts, not arbitrary shell fragments.

Examples:
- Minimal verification: `["test"]`
- Typical TypeScript project: `["lint", "test", "compile"]`
- Scaled repo with dedicated validation scripts: `["test:unit", "test:manifest", "typecheck"]`

Use short, deterministic scripts that give fast signal after edits.

atlasmind.autoVerifyTimeoutMs.description: Maximum time in milliseconds allowed for each automatic verification script.
atlasmind.autoVerifyTimeoutMs.markdownDescription:
Maximum time in milliseconds allowed for each automatic verification script. This timeout applies per script.

Examples:
- Fast local unit checks: `30000`
- Mixed test and lint pipeline: `120000`
- Large workspace with slower build validation: `300000`

Raise this only when your verification scripts are intentionally slower and still provide useful post-edit feedback.

atlasmind.chatSessionTurnLimit.description: How many recent chat turns AtlasMind carries forward into freeform requests.
atlasmind.chatSessionTurnLimit.markdownDescription:
How many recent chat turns AtlasMind carries forward into freeform requests. Higher values preserve more conversational continuity but increase prompt size.

Examples:
- Short, task-focused chats: `4`
- Default general use: `6`
- Long debugging sessions where prior decisions matter: `10` or higher

Increase this carefully in large team sessions so context remains relevant rather than noisy.

atlasmind.chatSessionContextChars.description: Maximum number of characters reserved for compacted session carry-forward context.
atlasmind.chatSessionContextChars.markdownDescription:
Maximum number of characters reserved for compacted session carry-forward context. This acts as the budget for summarized prior conversation.

Examples:
- Lightweight carry-forward: `1200`
- Default balance: `2500`
- Complex multi-step work with many assumptions to preserve: `4000` to `6000`

Use a higher value only if older conversation state is materially affecting correctness.

atlasmind.contextCompressionEnabled.description: Enable AtlasMind's prompt-context compaction path to reduce token volume and estimated spend.
atlasmind.contextCompressionEnabled.markdownDescription:
Enable AtlasMind's prompt-context compaction path. When this is on, AtlasMind trims carry-forward session context and summarizes retrieved memory/live evidence to stay within the current model budget. Turn it off if you want the rawer, less compact prompt path for debugging or comparison.

Examples:
- Keep the default efficiency path: `true`
- Compare or debug without compaction: `false`

atlasmind.projectApprovalFileThreshold.description: Estimated changed-file threshold that triggers /project approval gating.
atlasmind.projectApprovalFileThreshold.markdownDescription:
Estimated changed-file threshold that triggers `/project` approval gating. AtlasMind uses this with other planner heuristics to decide when work is large enough to require explicit confirmation.

Examples:
- Small utility repo: `6`
- Default general-use threshold: `12`
- Monorepo where broader edits are normal: `20` or `30`

Lower this in high-risk repositories where even moderate file churn should pause for review.

atlasmind.projectEstimatedFilesPerSubtas.description: Heuristic multiplier used to estimate changed files from the planned subtask count.
atlasmind.projectEstimatedFilesPerSubtas.markdownDescription:
Heuristic multiplier used to estimate changed files from the planned subtask count. Higher values make AtlasMind assume each subtask fans out across more files.

Examples:
- Tightly scoped codebase with isolated modules: `1`
- Typical service or extension repo: `2`
- Shared-platform or layered monorepo: `3` or `4`

Tune this to match how often a single planned step touches tests, docs, configs, and implementation together.

atlasmind.projectChangedFileReferenceLim.description: Maximum number of changed files surfaced as clickable references after /project runs.
atlasmind.projectChangedFileReferenceLim.markdownDescription:
Maximum number of changed files surfaced as clickable references after `/project` runs. This affects summary readability, not the actual set of changed files.

Examples:
- Compact summaries: `3`
- Default balance: `5`
- Review-heavy workflows where users want more direct navigation: `10`

Keep this lower if `/project` runs often touch many files and you want summaries to stay concise.

atlasmind.projectRunReportFolder.description: Relative folder for persisted /project run summary JSON reports.
atlasmind.projectRunReportFolder.markdownDescription:
Relative folder for persisted `/project` run summary JSON reports. AtlasMind stores operational summaries here for later review or tooling.

Examples:
- Default operational history: `project_memory/operations`
- Separate audit folder inside docs: `docs/atlasmind/runs`
- Centralized automation folder in a monorepo: `ops/atlasmind/run-reports`

Choose a stable relative path that fits your repo's review and retention practices.

atlasmind.projectDependencyMonitoringEna.description: Scaffold dependency monitoring defaults when AtlasMind bootstraps governance files for a project.
atlasmind.projectDependencyMonitoringEna.markdownDescription:
Scaffold dependency monitoring defaults when AtlasMind bootstraps governance files for a project. This controls whether bootstrap adds dependency-update automation and SSOT policy starter docs for Atlas-built repositories.

Examples:
- Team template repo where AtlasMind should always wire dependency review automation: `true`
- Minimal experimental repo where governance files stay manual: `false`

Disable this if your organization already provisions dependency automation elsewhere and you do not want AtlasMind creating update-policy files.

atlasmind.projectDependencyMonitoringPro.description: Dependency monitoring providers AtlasMind should scaffold for project governance baselines.
atlasmind.projectDependencyMonitoringPro.markdownDescription:
Dependency monitoring providers AtlasMind should scaffold for project governance baselines. AtlasMind currently supports Dependabot, Renovate, Snyk, and Azure DevOps-oriented pipeline scaffolding because those patterns are common in professional repositories and can be represented safely as checked-in config.

Examples:
- GitHub-native default: `["dependabot"]`
- Organizations standardized on Renovate: `["renovate"]`
- Security-driven workflow with Snyk plus Dependabot: `["dependabot", "snyk"]`
- Mixed enterprise rollout: `["dependabot", "renovate", "azure-devops"]`

If this list is empty while dependency monitoring is enabled, AtlasMind still scaffolds SSOT policy docs so teams can document a manual or externally managed review workflow.

atlasmind.projectDependencyMonitoringSch.description: Default cadence AtlasMind uses when scaffolding dependency monitoring automation.
atlasmind.projectDependencyMonitoringSch.markdownDescription:
Default cadence AtlasMind uses when scaffolding dependency monitoring automation. AtlasMind maps this into the generated Dependabot or Renovate configuration for Atlas-built projects.

Examples:
- Fast-moving security-sensitive services: `daily`
- Normal team workflow with predictable review windows: `weekly`
- Stable products that prefer fewer update PRs: `monthly`

Choose the slowest cadence that still lets your team review important updates before they become risky backlog.

atlasmind.projectDependencyMonitoringIss.description: Add a dependency review issue template when AtlasMind scaffolds project governance files.
atlasmind.projectDependencyMonitoringIss.markdownDescription:
Add a dependency review issue template when AtlasMind scaffolds project governance files. The template helps teams record approval decisions, exceptions, and follow-up work after automation detects dependency drift.

Examples:
- Review-heavy engineering org that tracks every deferred or major update: `true`
- Lightweight personal repo with no formal review tickets: `false`

Keep this on when updates must be reviewed by multiple people or linked to compliance evidence.

atlasmind.loop.enabled.description: Enable the autonomous goal-seeking Mission Loop (the /loop chat command and Mission Control panel).
atlasmind.loop.enabled.markdownDescription:
Enable the autonomous goal-seeking **Mission Loop** — the `/loop` chat command and the Mission Control panel. When disabled, AtlasMind will not start any looping run.

The loop plans, executes, and re-evaluates progress toward a goal across multiple iterations, stopping when the goal is met or a guardrail confines progress. It is safety-first: every run is bounded by a closed parameter envelope and pauses for approval at configured checkpoints.

Examples:
- Allow autonomous loops: `true`
- Lock the feature off in a restricted workspace: `false`

atlasmind.loop.defaultMaxIterations.description: Default hard cap on Mission Loop iterations before the loop stops.
atlasmind.loop.defaultMaxIterations.markdownDescription:
Default hard cap on Mission Loop iterations before the loop stops, regardless of progress. This is one of the closed-envelope guardrails.

Examples:
- Quick scoped task: `3`
- Default balance: `8`
- Larger multi-step effort: `15`

Lower this in unattended or cost-sensitive environments.

atlasmind.loop.defaultMaxCostUsd.description: Default hard ceiling (USD) on cumulative Mission Loop cost.
atlasmind.loop.defaultMaxCostUsd.markdownDescription:
Default hard ceiling, in USD, on the cumulative cost of a single Mission Loop run. Enforced before every iteration on top of `atlasmind.dailyCostLimitUsd`.

Examples:
- Tight personal cap: `1`
- Default balance: `5`
- Larger sanctioned run: `20`

atlasmind.loop.defaultMaxTokens.description: Default hard ceiling on cumulative (input + output) tokens for a Mission Loop run.
atlasmind.loop.defaultMaxTokens.markdownDescription:
Default hard ceiling on cumulative (input + output) tokens across a Mission Loop run. A backstop alongside the cost and iteration caps.

Examples:
- Small task: `300000`
- Default balance: `2000000`
- Large effort: `5000000`

atlasmind.loop.defaultMaxDurationMinutes.description: Default hard wall-clock cap (minutes) for a Mission Loop run.
atlasmind.loop.defaultMaxDurationMinutes.markdownDescription:
Default hard wall-clock cap, in minutes, for a Mission Loop run. The loop stops at the next iteration boundary once this is exceeded.

Examples:
- Short supervised run: `10`
- Default balance: `30`
- Long unattended run: `120`

atlasmind.loop.maxConsecutiveNoProgress.description: Stop the Mission Loop after this many consecutive no-progress iterations.
atlasmind.loop.maxConsecutiveNoProgress.markdownDescription:
Stop the Mission Loop after this many consecutive iterations in which the goal evaluator reports no measurable progress. Prevents the loop from burning budget while spinning on a problem it cannot move forward.

Examples:
- Fail fast: `1`
- Default balance: `2`
- Give the loop more room to recover: `3`

atlasmind.loop.checkpointEveryNIteration.description: Pause the Mission Loop for approval every N iterations (0 disables cadence checkpoints).
atlasmind.loop.checkpointEveryNIteration.markdownDescription:
Pause the Mission Loop for a human approval checkpoint every N iterations. Set to `0` to disable iteration-cadence checkpoints (budget-fraction checkpoints still apply).

Examples:
- Approve every iteration: `1`
- Default balance: `3`
- Fewer interruptions: `5`

Checkpoints are deny-by-default: if no one approves, the loop stops safely.

atlasmind.loop.checkpointAtBudgetFractio.description: Pause for approval the first time cumulative spend crosses this fraction (0..1) of the cost budget.
atlasmind.loop.checkpointAtBudgetFractio.markdownDescription:
Pause the Mission Loop for an approval checkpoint the first time cumulative spend crosses this fraction (0..1) of the cost budget.

Examples:
- Check in early: `0.5`
- Default balance: `0.75`
- Only near the cap: `0.9`

atlasmind.loop.requireApprovalBeforeWrit.description: Require an approval checkpoint before any Mission Loop iteration that may write files or commit.
atlasmind.loop.requireApprovalBeforeWrit.markdownDescription:
Require an approval checkpoint before any Mission Loop iteration expected to write files or commit. Strongest safety posture; most interruptive.

Examples:
- Trust the loop within its other guardrails: `false`
- Review every write batch: `true`

atlasmind.loop.allowDiscovery.description: Allow the Mission Loop to synthesize new agents/skills and use Agentic Resource Discovery to fill capability gaps (always behind existing approval gates).
atlasmind.loop.allowDiscovery.markdownDescription:
Allow the Mission Loop to fill capability gaps by synthesizing new agents/skills and using Agentic Resource Discovery (ARD). New capabilities always pass the existing approval gates before use; the loop prefers already-registered capabilities first.

Examples:
- Let the loop learn what it needs: `true`
- Restrict to existing capabilities only: `false`

atlasmind.loop.goalAchievedConfidenceThr.description: Minimum goal-evaluator confidence (0..1) required to accept an 'achieved' verdict and stop the loop successfully.
atlasmind.loop.goalAchievedConfidenceThr.markdownDescription:
Minimum confidence (0..1) the goal evaluator must report before an `achieved` verdict is accepted and the loop stops successfully. Below this, the loop keeps iterating — a low-confidence evaluator can never falsely declare success.

Examples:
- Stop more readily: `0.6`
- Default balance: `0.7`
- Demand high certainty: `0.85`

atlasmind.toolWebhookEnabled.description: Enable outbound webhook delivery for Atlas tool execution events.
atlasmind.toolWebhookEnabled.markdownDescription:
Enable outbound webhook delivery for Atlas tool execution events. When enabled, AtlasMind sends selected tool lifecycle events to the configured webhook endpoint.

Examples:
- Local-only development with no external observers: `false`
- Team telemetry or audit pipeline: `true`

Only enable this when you have an approved HTTPS endpoint and clear expectations about what execution metadata may leave the editor.

atlasmind.toolWebhookUrl.description: HTTPS endpoint that receives Atlas tool execution webhook payloads.
atlasmind.toolWebhookUrl.markdownDescription:
HTTPS endpoint that receives Atlas tool execution webhook payloads. Leave empty unless `atlasmind.toolWebhookEnabled` is turned on.

Examples:
- Internal event collector: `https://ops.example.com/atlasmind/webhooks`
- Local integration test tunnel: `https://1234abcd.ngrok.app/hooks/atlasmind`

Prefer a dedicated ingestion endpoint for scaled deployments so AtlasMind events stay separated from unrelated webhooks.

atlasmind.toolWebhookTimeoutMs.markdownDescription:
Webhook request timeout in milliseconds. This limits how long AtlasMind waits for the webhook receiver before treating delivery as timed out.

Examples:
- Low-latency internal service: `3000`
- Default general use: `5000`
- Cross-region or heavily filtered ingress path: `10000`

Do not raise this unnecessarily, or slow webhook infrastructure can start delaying the editor experience.

atlasmind.toolWebhookEvents.description: Selected tool webhook event names to emit.
atlasmind.toolWebhookEvents.markdownDescription:
Selected tool webhook event names to emit. Choose the smallest set that satisfies your observability or audit needs.

Available events:
- `tool.started`
- `tool.completed`
- `tool.failed`
- `tool.test`

Examples:
- Minimal audit trail: `["tool.failed"]`
- Basic lifecycle monitoring: `["tool.started", "tool.completed", "tool.failed"]`
- Integration testing of receivers: include `tool.test` temporarily

atlasmind.experimentalSkillLearningEnabl.description: Enable Atlas-generated custom skill drafts. Warning: this sends additional model requests and generated code still requires manual safety review.
atlasmind.experimentalSkillLearningEnabl.markdownDescription:
Enable Atlas-generated custom skill drafts. This feature increases model usage and the generated artifacts still require manual review before they are trusted or committed.

Examples:
- Production or regulated workspace: `false`
- Sandbox for experimenting with new skills: `true`

Treat this as an assisted authoring feature, not an autonomous trust boundary.

atlasmind.dailyCostLimitUsd.description: Daily cost limit in USD. Set to 0 to disable. AtlasMind will warn you when 80% and 100% of this limit is reached.
atlasmind.dailyCostLimitUsd.markdownDescription:
Daily cost limit in USD. Set this to `0` to disable the cap. AtlasMind warns at 80% usage and again at 100%.

Examples:
- Unlimited personal experimentation: `0`
- Individual guardrail for a paid account: `5` or `10`
- Shared team budget with tighter daily control per developer: `20` or another agreed cap

Use this with `budgetMode` to combine soft routing preferences and a hard spend boundary.
