atlasmind.displayCurrency.markdownDescription:
Currency used for **all** cost displays across AtlasMind. Defaults to `USD`. Pick a specific currency and it is applied app-wide (dashboards, chat, Mission Loop, etc.), or choose `auto` to detect from your OS locale. Underlying costs are always stored in USD; exchange rates are fetched at startup with a 24-hour cache.

Examples:
- Default: `USD`
- UK developer: `GBP`
- European team: `EUR`
- Japanese users: `JPY`
- Detect from OS locale: `auto`

atlasmind.voice.ttsEnabled.description: Automatically speak @atlas freeform responses aloud using the Voice Panel TTS engine.
atlasmind.voice.ttsEnabled.markdownDescription:
Automatically speak `@atlas` freeform responses aloud using the Voice Panel TTS engine. This affects spoken playback, not text generation.

Examples:
- Hands-free coding or accessibility workflow: `true`
- Quiet office or text-only use: `false`

atlasmind.voice.sttEnabled.description: Show a voice input button in the Voice Panel (STT requires microphone access).
atlasmind.voice.sttEnabled.markdownDescription:
Show a voice input button in the Voice Panel. Speech-to-text requires microphone access and browser or platform support.

Examples:
- Voice-first workflow: `true`
- Locked-down desktop without microphone permissions: `false`

atlasmind.voice.hostSpeechEnabled.description: Use the operating system's built-in speech engine (host-side) for text-to-speech instead of the in-panel Web Speech engine. Works without the Voice Panel open and uses no network or API key.
atlasmind.voice.hostSpeechEnabled.markdownDescription:
Use the operating system's built-in speech engine for text-to-speech instead of the in-panel Web Speech engine.

When enabled, AtlasMind speaks via the host OS engine (Windows SAPI through PowerShell, macOS `say`, or Linux `espeak-ng`). This runs entirely on-device — no network and no API key — and works even when the Voice Panel is closed. An ElevenLabs API key, when configured, still takes priority. On Linux, `espeak-ng` must be installed.

Examples:
- Fully local, hands-free playback without opening the panel: `true`
- Prefer the in-webview Web Speech voices: `false`

enumDescriptions: Use on-device Whisper where it can be provisioned (Windows, or any platform with whisperCliPath set), otherwise the Web Speech API.
Always use the in-webview Web Speech API (may route audio to a cloud service and is often unavailable in the editor runtime).
Always use on-device Whisper transcription.
atlasmind.voice.sttEngine.description: Speech-to-text engine for the Voice Panel: on-device Whisper or the in-webview Web Speech API.
atlasmind.voice.sttEngine.markdownDescription:
Speech-to-text engine for the Voice Panel.

- `auto` (default): use on-device **Whisper** where it can be provisioned (Windows auto-downloads a verified `whisper-cli`; other platforms need `atlasmind.voice.whisperCliPath`), otherwise fall back to the Web Speech API.
- `local`: always use on-device Whisper. Audio never leaves your machine; the model (and, on Windows, the CLI) are downloaded once and SHA-256-verified.
- `webspeech`: always use the in-webview Web Speech API. Note this may stream audio to a cloud service and is frequently unavailable in the editor runtime.

atlasmind.voice.whisperCliPath.description: Path to an installed whisper.cpp 'whisper-cli' executable for on-device speech-to-text. Required on macOS/Linux (e.g. via `brew install whisper-cpp`); on Windows a verified build is downloaded automatically when left empty.
atlasmind.voice.whisperCliPath.markdownDescription:
Absolute path to an installed whisper.cpp `whisper-cli` executable used for on-device speech-to-text.

On **Windows x64** this can be left empty — AtlasMind downloads an official, SHA-256-verified `whisper-cli` on first use. On **macOS/Linux** there is no official prebuilt binary, so install whisper.cpp (for example `brew install whisper-cpp`) and point this setting at the resulting `whisper-cli`.

atlasmind.voice.rate.description: Speech synthesis rate. 1.0 is normal speed; 0.5 is half speed; 2.0 is double speed.
atlasmind.voice.rate.markdownDescription:
Speech synthesis rate. `1.0` is normal speed, `0.5` is half speed, and `2.0` is double speed.

Examples:
- Accessibility or careful listening: `0.8`
- Default conversational playback: `1.0`
- Fast review of long responses: `1.25` or `1.5`

atlasmind.voice.pitch.description: Speech synthesis pitch. 1.0 is the default pitch.
atlasmind.voice.pitch.markdownDescription:
Speech synthesis pitch. `1.0` is the default pitch for the selected voice.

Examples:
- Lower, flatter speech profile: `0.8`
- Default voice output: `1.0`
- Brighter or more animated playback: `1.2`

Use this mainly for comfort and intelligibility rather than correctness.

atlasmind.voice.volume.description: Speech synthesis volume (0 = silent, 1 = full volume).
atlasmind.voice.volume.markdownDescription:
Speech synthesis volume where `0` is silent and `1` is full volume.

Examples:
- Shared office or quiet environment: `0.3` to `0.5`
- Normal headset use: `0.8` to `1.0`
- Muted while keeping TTS enabled for quick toggling: `0`

atlasmind.voice.language.description: BCP 47 language tag for voice synthesis and recognition (e.g. 'en-US', 'fr-FR'). Leave empty to use the browser/OS default.
atlasmind.voice.language.markdownDescription:
BCP 47 language tag for voice synthesis and recognition, such as `en-US` or `fr-FR`. Leave empty to use the browser or OS default.

Examples:
- US English: `en-US`
- British English: `en-GB`
- French (France): `fr-FR`
- Default system language: empty string

Set this explicitly in shared environments where predictable voice language matters.

atlasmind.voice.inputDeviceId.description: Preferred microphone device id for voice input. Leave empty to use the system default microphone.
atlasmind.voice.inputDeviceId.markdownDescription:
Preferred microphone device id for voice input, selected from the **Devices** page of the Voice Panel. Leave empty to use the system default microphone.

This is used for the microphone-permission preflight and is honored by backends that can target a specific input device. Browser Web Speech recognition may still follow the OS or browser default microphone.

atlasmind.voice.outputDeviceId.description: Preferred audio output device id for voice playback. Leave empty to use the system default speaker.
atlasmind.voice.outputDeviceId.markdownDescription:
Preferred audio output device id for voice playback, selected from the **Devices** page of the Voice Panel. Leave empty to use the system default speaker.

Output routing applies to ElevenLabs audio playback when the webview runtime supports `setSinkId`. Browser speech synthesis still follows the browser or OS default output device.

atlasmind.voice.elevenLabsVoiceId.description: ElevenLabs voice id used for server-side text-to-speech. Leave empty to use the default demo voice.
atlasmind.voice.elevenLabsVoiceId.markdownDescription:
ElevenLabs voice id used for server-side text-to-speech when an ElevenLabs API key is configured in Specialist Integrations. Leave empty to use the default demo voice (`Rachel`).

Find voice ids in your ElevenLabs voice library. This setting has no effect unless an ElevenLabs API key is present.

atlasmind.maxToolIterations.description: Maximum tool-call loop iterations per agent turn.
atlasmind.maxToolIterations.markdownDescription:
Maximum tool-call loop iterations per agent turn. This limits how many sequential rounds of tool use the agent can perform before it must stop and answer.

Examples:
- Conservative environment: `5`
- Default balance: `10`
- Complex workflows that genuinely need longer tool chains: `15` to `20`

Raise this carefully, because higher values can increase latency and unintended automation depth.

atlasmind.maxToolCallsPerTurn.description: Maximum parallel tool calls the model may issue in a single turn.
atlasmind.maxToolCallsPerTurn.markdownDescription:
Maximum parallel tool calls the model may issue in a single turn. This caps fan-out when the model wants to gather or verify data quickly.

Examples:
- Minimal concurrency for predictable behavior: `3`
- Default general use: `8`
- Large codebase exploration with many independent reads: `12` or `16`

Higher values can improve speed for read-heavy work but may produce noisier or more expensive turns.

atlasmind.toolExecutionTimeoutMs.markdownDescription:
Per-tool execution timeout in milliseconds. If a tool call exceeds this limit, AtlasMind treats it as timed out.

Examples:
- Very fast local commands only: `5000`
- Default mixed workload: `15000`
- Slower file-system or network-backed tools: `30000`

Tune this alongside tool approval and webhook settings so slow integrations do not degrade the interactive experience.

atlasmind.providerTimeoutMs.description: Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for a model provider response.
atlasmind.providerTimeoutMs.markdownDescription:
Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for a model provider response. This covers the provider round-trip, not local tool execution.

Examples:
- Fast local or LAN-hosted models: `15000`
- Default cloud-provider balance: `30000`
- Slower premium reasoning models or distant regions: `45000` to `60000`

Use a higher timeout when you intentionally allow slower reasoning models through `speedMode` or provider-specific routing.

atlasmind.remote.enabled.description: ⚠️ Not the control that starts or stops remote control — this setting currently has no effect. The remote-control server starts only when you run the AtlasMind remote-control command and approve this workspace, and it stops when you disable it there. Turning this off does not disable remote control.
atlasmind.remote.enabled.markdownDescription:
**This is not the control that starts or stops remote control, and it currently has no effect.**

The remote-control server starts only when you run the AtlasMind remote-control command *and* approve this workspace at the prompt; it stops when you disable it from the same place. Setting this to `false` does **not** disable remote control — check the status-bar indicator, which reflects what is actually running.

enumDescriptions: Same-machine pairing: a web client on this machine connects with the pairing token.
SSO gateway: an authenticated Cloudflare Worker + tunnel front the server; the browser's login is its identity.
atlasmind.remote.mode.description: Transport and authentication mode for the remote-control server.
atlasmind.remote.mode.markdownDescription:
Transport and authentication mode for the remote-control server.

- **`localhost`** (default) — a same-machine web client (vscode.dev / github.dev / code-server) pairs with the token over `ws://127.0.0.1`.
- **`gateway`** — the server is fronted by an SSO-gated Cloudflare Worker and a Cloudflare Tunnel, so you can reach it from a browser signed into your platform login. The server authenticates each connection by the `x-atlas-origin-secret` header the Worker injects (reusing the pairing-token secret) instead of an in-band token, so the browser never holds a token. Pin `atlasmind.remote.port` to a stable value so the tunnel target stays fixed. Run **AtlasMind: Enable Remote Control (Gateway)** to switch on this mode. See the Remote Control documentation for the full topology and security model.

atlasmind.remote.port.description: Localhost port for the remote-control server. Use 0 to pick a free port automatically.
atlasmind.remote.port.markdownDescription:
Localhost port for the remote-control server. AtlasMind binds the server to `127.0.0.1` on this port.

Examples:
- Pick a free port automatically (recommended): `0`
- Pin a stable port so the web client's saved URL keeps working: `38917`

Only pin a port if you need the `ws://localhost:PORT` URL to stay constant across restarts.

atlasmind.ci.localRunner.enabled.description: Allow the Pipeline dashboard to start one ephemeral GitHub Actions runner inside Docker for an already-queued trusted job. Off by default.
atlasmind.ci.localRunner.enabled.markdownDescription:
**Off by default and machine-scoped.** Allows AtlasMind's Pipeline dashboard to lend this machine to exactly one already-queued GitHub Actions job through an ephemeral Docker container.

AtlasMind does not dispatch or rerun CI. Before starting it requires an owner-triggered run for the current commit, a trusted-branch-only workflow, read-only permissions, no secrets, SHA-pinned actions, a unique custom label, and an explicit confirmation. The container receives no host mount, Docker socket, GPU, workspace credential, or persistent volume.

atlasmind.ci.localRunner.workflowFile.description: Trusted GitHub Actions workflow filename inside .github/workflows. AtlasMind validates the committed file before every local runner start.
atlasmind.ci.localRunner.workflowFile.markdownDescription:
The one workflow file the local executor may serve, as a filename inside `.github/workflows`. This is machine-scoped so an untrusted workspace cannot silently point your machine at another job.

The filename is only a selector, never authority: AtlasMind re-reads and validates the committed workflow before every start.

atlasmind.ci.localRunner.trustedBranch.description: Only queued runs on this exact branch and current commit may claim the local runner.
atlasmind.ci.localRunner.trustedBranch.markdownDescription: The exact branch the local executor trusts. The workflow, queued run, current checkout, repository condition, and `github.ref` job condition must all agree with this value. Machine-scoped so repository configuration cannot broaden the trust boundary.

atlasmind.ci.localRunner.runnerLabel.description: Dedicated no-default-labels runner label. {arch} expands to x64 or arm64 from Docker's actual architecture.
atlasmind.ci.localRunner.runnerLabel.markdownDescription:
The dedicated routing label registered with `--no-default-labels`. `{arch}` expands from Docker's actual engine architecture (`x64` or `arm64`), not from a guess about the host.

AtlasMind refuses to start if this label appears in another local workflow or if a runner with the label is already registered. A label routes work; the workflow and queued-run checks authorise it.

atlasmind.ci.localRunner.image.description: Runner container image. AtlasMind auto-pulls only digest-pinned references and always runs the resolved immutable image id.
atlasmind.ci.localRunner.image.markdownDescription:
The runner container image for this machine. The shipped value is an immutable GitHub Actions runner digest. AtlasMind auto-pulls only a `@sha256:` reference and then runs Docker's resolved image id.

A locally built tag is accepted only when it is already installed; AtlasMind resolves it to an image id before use, so a tag cannot move between confirmation and start. This supports locally trusted CA images without teaching AtlasMind the certificate or mounting it from the host.

atlasmind.ci.localRunner.maxCpus.description: Maximum logical CPUs the local runner container may use. AtlasMind may allocate less to preserve at least 25% for the host.
atlasmind.ci.localRunner.maxCpus.markdownDescription: Upper CPU limit for the local runner container. AtlasMind reads both host and Docker-engine capacity, preserves at least 25% for the desktop, and uses the lower of the calculated allowance and this cap. It refuses to run below two CPUs.

atlasmind.ci.localRunner.maxMemoryGb.description: Maximum memory in GB the local runner container may use. AtlasMind may allocate less to preserve at least 25% for the host.
atlasmind.ci.localRunner.maxMemoryGb.markdownDescription: Upper memory limit for the local runner container. AtlasMind reads both host and Docker-engine capacity, preserves at least 25% (and at least 2 GB) for the desktop, and uses the lower of the calculated allowance and this cap. It refuses to run below 4 GB and disables container swap.

enumDescriptions: Recommended: stop Docker Desktop only when AtlasMind started it for this run.
Always leave Docker Desktop open after the runner exits.
Stop Docker Desktop after the runner exits, even if it was already open. AtlasMind still refuses while another container is running.
atlasmind.ci.localRunner.shutdownPolicy.description: Whether AtlasMind closes Docker Desktop after the ephemeral runner exits.
atlasmind.ci.localRunner.shutdownPolicy.markdownDescription:
Controls Docker Desktop cleanup after the ephemeral runner exits.

- **`ifStartedByAtlasMind`** (recommended) — close it only when AtlasMind opened it for this run.
- **`never`** — leave it open.
- **`always`** — close it even if it was already open.

Every policy has the same hard guard: AtlasMind leaves Docker open if it cannot inventory containers or if any unrelated container is running. It never starts or stops a Linux system Docker service.

atlasmind.workflow.enabled.description: Master switch for the guided GitHub workflow. Off by default: the Workflow dashboard still teaches and measures, but AtlasMind takes no action on your repository.
atlasmind.workflow.enabled.markdownDescription:
**Off by default — this is the master switch.**

With it off, the Workflow page of the Project Dashboard is fully usable: it explains all eight stages, shows how far your repository has got, and charts the numbers. It simply never *acts*.

Turning it on does not, by itself, let AtlasMind do anything. The effective automation level for any stage is the **minimum** of four independent gates:

1. this master switch,
2. `#atlasmind.workflow.maxAutomationLevel#` — your personal ceiling,
3. the matching capability switch (`allowIssueWrites`, `allowPullRequestWrites`, `allowReleaseWrites`),
4. the level declared for that stage in the project's workflow configuration.

All four default closed, which is what makes full automation *possible* without ever making it the default. See [the specification](https://github.com/JoelBondoux/AtlasMind/blob/main/docs/guided-github-workflow.md).

atlasmind.workflow.archetype.description: What kind of project this is. Changes CI steps, release model, testing recommendations, expected documentation, and refactor advice. Empty means undeclared — AtlasMind detects a suggestion but never acts on it as a decision.
atlasmind.workflow.archetype.markdownDescription:
**What kind of project this is** — the single biggest lever on how the guided workflow specialises.

A game, a website, a library and a CLI do not share a CI pipeline, a release mechanism, a testing strategy, or the same idea of what counts as technical debt. Declaring the shape switches all six.

**Detection suggests; this setting decides.** AtlasMind reads your manifests and proposes a shape, but a project deliberately declared one thing while its dependencies look like another is a *decision*, not a mistake — so the declaration always wins, and the Workflow page shows both when they differ.

Leaving this empty is honest rather than broken: `generic` behaviour applies, and the page says the shape is undeclared instead of pretending to know. **A wrong archetype is worse than none**, because it asks for evidence the project will never produce and creates a permanent gap — which teaches people to ignore gaps.

Use `#atlasmind.workflow.traits#` for facts that cut across shapes, such as shipping binaries or handling personal data.

atlasmind.workflow.traits.description: Facts about this project that cut across its shape — ships binaries, publishes a package, handles personal data, and so on. Each adds expectations on top of the archetype rather than replacing them.
atlasmind.workflow.traits.markdownDescription:
Facts that cut across project shapes, so the archetype list does not have to grow a new member every time something ships differently.

A Shopify theme is a `website` that happens to be **platform-hosted**; a VS Code extension is a `library` that is both **platform-hosted** and **published**. Modelling those as their own archetypes would multiply the list per platform.

Traits are **additive**: each one adds CI steps, documentation expectations and refactor heuristics on top of the archetype's, and never removes any. If a trait needed to *remove* an expectation, that would be a sign it should have been its own archetype.

- `handles-personal-data` adds a secret-and-personal-data scan and a privacy document, because anything committed is effectively permanent.
- `is-published-package` adds a publish dry-run, because a published version number cannot be reused.
- `ships-binaries` adds an artifact smoke check, because a binary that builds but does not start fails only on a user's machine.

atlasmind.workflow.profile.description: Which workflow profile to teach and measure against. 'solo' expects one person to be author, reviewer and releaser; 'studio' expects authorship and approval to be separable.
atlasmind.workflow.profile.markdownDescription:
Which profile the Workflow page teaches against.

- **`solo`** — one human is author, reviewer and releaser. Zero required approvals, because requiring your own approval is theatre and trains you to dismiss a gate. CI becomes the reviewer, which is why its checks stop being optional.
- **`studio`** — 3–10 people, authorship and approval separable. At least one approver distinct from the author. This is the one place the two profiles differ in *kind* rather than in degree.
- **`custom`** — you have declared your own stage values and neither preset should be assumed.

A profile **seeds**; it does not govern. Once a project's workflow configuration exists, that file wins, and changing this setting never silently rewrites it.

atlasmind.workflow.maxAutomationLevel.description: Your personal ceiling on what AtlasMind may do in the workflow. Can only lower the project's declared level, never raise it. Defaults to 'observe' — read and display only.
atlasmind.workflow.maxAutomationLevel.markdownDescription:
**Your personal ceiling. Defaults to `observe`.**

Five rungs, each strictly more capable than the last:

| Rung | AtlasMind may |
|---|---|
| `off` | nothing |
| `observe` | read state, compute metrics, display |
| `draft` | produce an artifact and show it |
| `propose` | act, after an explicit confirmation naming the repository and the exact action |
| `auto` | act unattended, still inside the stage's gates |

This setting can only **lower** the effective level, never raise it. You may run the whole workflow at `observe` on your machine while the repository declares `propose`; you cannot run at `auto` if the repository says otherwise.

Some things never automate at any rung: force-pushing, deleting a tag or release, re-running a CI job, editing a CI workflow file, and merging a dependency update.

atlasmind.workflow.allowIssueWrites.description: Allow AtlasMind to create, comment on, edit, close or reopen GitHub issues. Off by default; every write still asks for confirmation naming the repository and the exact action.
atlasmind.workflow.allowIssueWrites.markdownDescription:
**Off by default.** Permits stage 1 (Planning & Issue Intake) and stage 7 (Maintenance) to write to your issue tracker.

Even with this on, every write is outward-facing and public, so each one asks for a confirmation naming the repository and the exact action. AtlasMind never auto-closes an issue — closing somebody's report is a social act, not a cleanup task.

Requires `#atlasmind.workflow.enabled#` and a stage level of `propose` or higher.

atlasmind.workflow.allowPullRequestWrite.description: Allow AtlasMind to create pull requests, post reviews, and merge. Off by default; every write still asks for confirmation.
atlasmind.workflow.allowPullRequestWrite.markdownDescription:
**Off by default.** Permits stage 4 (Pull Requests & Reviews) to write.

A pull request is a public proposal, so every creation, review and merge asks for confirmation first. Note that review comments arriving *from* GitHub are treated as untrusted input regardless of this setting — anyone who can comment can write text designed to be read as an instruction, so review bodies are always sanitized and fenced before an agent sees them.

Requires `#atlasmind.workflow.enabled#` and a stage level of `propose` or higher.

atlasmind.workflow.allowReleaseWrites.description: Allow AtlasMind to prepare releases — version bump, changelog entry, tag and GitHub Release. Off by default; tagging and publishing stay human-triggered.
atlasmind.workflow.allowReleaseWrites.markdownDescription:
**Off by default.** Permits stage 6 (Release Automation) to write.

Even with this on, `draft` is the maximum in the shipped default: AtlasMind prepares the version bump and the changelog entry, and **tagging and publishing stay human-triggered**.

Release notes are the changelog section for that version, *verbatim* — never generated by a model. A release note is a durable public claim, and the changelog is where that claim was already reviewed.

Requires `#atlasmind.workflow.enabled#`.

atlasmind.workflow.allowProtectedRefWrit.description: Allow AtlasMind to write to a protected branch. Off by default and rarely correct — a protected branch exists precisely so that changes reach it only through a reviewed pull request.
atlasmind.workflow.allowProtectedRefWrit.markdownDescription:
**Off by default, and this is a hard ceiling rather than an ordinary preference.**

A protected branch exists precisely so that changes reach it only through a pull request that passed its checks. Enabling this removes the protection at the moment it would have helped, so it should be enabled only for a specific, temporary reason.

With this off, `auto` is *unreachable* for any stage whose base is protected — not discouraged, unreachable.

AtlasMind never force-pushes regardless of this setting. Where a force is unavoidable it uses a lease, and to a protected branch it refuses outright.

atlasmind.acp.toolsEnabled.description: Let subscription agents act — make ACP agents eligible for tool-backed work and automatically allow their own tools without prompting for each operation. Off by default.
atlasmind.acp.toolsEnabled.markdownDescription:
**Let subscription agents act.** **Off by default.** Makes an ACP agent — a Claude or ChatGPT subscription driven over the [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com) — eligible for work that needs actions, then lets it use its own tools to edit files, run commands, search, or fetch.

Turning this on is standing authorization for ACP tool operations. AtlasMind separately authorizes the exact provider request only when the selected turn genuinely needs native tools; ordinary completions remain settings-isolated, receive no configured MCP servers, and have no permission policy even while this switch is on.

On an authorized tool-backed turn AtlasMind automatically answers each permission request without showing another prompt. Every request is still classified and written to the AtlasMind output log. AtlasMind answers only `allow_once` on the wire and never accepts an agent's `allow_always` option, so no permanent grant is stored inside software AtlasMind cannot display or revoke. Switching this setting off stops future operations, including requests from an already-running session.

Two things worth knowing before turning this on:

- **The work happens inside the agent's process, not inside AtlasMind.** The agent performs operations with whatever user-level access its process already has.
- **This authorizes edits, commands, network fetches, and unrecognised ACP operations for routed tool-backed turns.** Enable it only for agents and workspaces you trust; leave it off for completion-only use.

With this off, ACP agents remain eligible for chat, code, and reasoning that needs no tools; tool-backed work routes to a provider that can accept AtlasMind function calls. See also `#atlasmind.acp.mcpServers#` and `#atlasmind.acp.hideConsoleWindows#`.

atlasmind.acp.mcpServers.description: Names of MCP servers ACP agents may use. Empty by default — an agent gets no MCP servers unless you name them here. Requires atlasmind.acp.toolsEnabled.
atlasmind.acp.mcpServers.markdownDescription:
Which of your MCP servers an ACP agent may connect to, **by name**. Empty by default, and only consulted when `#atlasmind.acp.toolsEnabled#` is on.

Naming a server here means the agent's process launches that server's command with its environment. Two kinds are held back even when listed, and AtlasMind says so in its output channel:

- **Servers whose credentials live in VS Code SecretStorage.** Forwarding those would copy a key you gave *AtlasMind* into another vendor's process as a side effect of ticking a box. Such a server keeps working normally through AtlasMind's own tools.
- **HTTP/SSE servers**, whose headers carry bearer tokens. Only stdio servers are shared.

atlasmind.debt.markers.markdownDescription:
Extra comment markers the tech-debt scan looks for, on top of the built-in `TODO`, `FIXME`, `HACK` and `XXX`.

Write each as `NAME` or `NAME:severity`, for example `["DEBT", "REVISIT:high", "NOTE:low"]`. An unqualified marker is graded **medium** — somebody who bothered to declare a marker is asserting that something is wrong, which is the same reason `FIXME` outranks `TODO`.

Each marker becomes a *declared rule*, named on every entry it grades and published in the rule table of `tech-debt.md`. That is what keeps the register comparable: a grade you can look up is a grade you can argue with.

The built-in four cannot be redefined. Letting a project grade its own `TODO` as high would make two projects' registers incomparable, which is the one thing the rule table exists to prevent. A marker mentioning a credential is still graded high whatever you called it.

Markers are letters, digits, underscore and hyphen only, and at most 20 are read.

atlasmind.testingPolicyOverride.description: Testing methodology the Settings dashboard reports as this project's policy. Empty means Red-Green TDD, the default. Read by the Testing page since 0.46 but never declared, so it could not be found in Settings.

atlasmind.ideation.crossProjectPaths.description: Absolute paths to other AtlasMind projects whose ideation boards may be read for cross-project context. At most three are consulted, and nothing is ever written to another project.

atlasmind.lens.live.enabled.description: Master switch for the live lenses (Live Contract Drift, Service Reachability, Live Data Trust), which compare what your repository declares against what a running service actually serves. Off by default: a probe leaves this machine and reaches a system somebody else operates. AtlasMind reads shape only — the schema a service publishes, an information_schema listing — never a row, never a record, never a field value, and it never writes. Services are declared in .atlasmind/lens-endpoints.json; nothing is probed until you ask.

atlasmind.lens.live.allowedStages.markdownDescription: Which declared environments a probe may reach. Production is deliberately absent from the default, and an endpoint that does not state its stage counts as `unknown`, which is treated as production. Adding `production` or `unknown` does not skip the confirmation: those endpoints still require you to type the endpoint's label before each probe. An empty list means no stage is allowed, and is honoured as written.

atlasmind.research.enabled.description: Master switch for research scans, which ask questions about the world outside this repository (competition, customers, technology, feature gaps, market, funding, regulation). Off by default: a scan reaches the network and spends on a model. Findings are recorded in project_memory/analysis/research.json, and a claim with no retrievable source is stored as a question rather than as evidence.

enumDescriptions: Tell you when a scan is due. Nothing runs.
Draft the scan brief when one is due. Running it is still a click.
Run a due scan on window activation, inside the declared spend cap. Findings still land as open and need triage.
atlasmind.research.automationLevel.description: The ceiling every individual scan's automation level is capped by. A scan may request more and will be reduced to this, with the reduction stated. AtlasMind never files a decision on your behalf at any level.

atlasmind.research.scans.description: Per-scan overrides, keyed by scan id (competition, customer, technology, feature, market, funding, regulatory). Each value may set `enabled` (boolean), `cadenceDays` (number) and `automationLevel` (observe/propose/auto). A scan is off until switched on here. Unknown ids are ignored.

enumDescriptions: Use the best source available: EXA, then a connected MCP search tool, then the built-in fetch.
EXA web search. Requires an EXA API key in the Specialist Integrations panel.
A connected MCP server exposing a search or fetch tool.
The built-in Fetch URL skill. It can read a page you name but cannot find one, so scans that need discovery will report what they could not assess.
No source. External scans will refuse to run rather than answering from the model's own recollection.
atlasmind.research.searchSource.description: Where research scans look. With no usable source AtlasMind reports that it could not look — it never falls back to what a model already believed.

atlasmind.research.monthlySpendCapUsd.description: The most automatic research runs may spend per month. 0 (the default) means no scan may run on its own, whatever its automation level — turning research on and letting it run unattended are deliberately two separate decisions. Scans you start yourself are not capped here.

atlasmind.instructions.verifyOnCommit.description: Refuse a commit when an AI instruction file has a stale AtlasMind block. Verify only — never edits files.
atlasmind.instructions.verifyOnCommit.markdownDescription:
Before each commit, check that the AtlasMind-managed blocks in your AI instruction files
(`CLAUDE.md`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `AGENTS.md`, Cursor, Cline, Gemini,
Windsurf, Aider) still match the documents they were generated from.

**On by default, and verify-only: the check never edits a file.** It refuses the commit and
names the command that fixes it — the same way this repository already treats a missing
version bump. That is deliberate rather than cautious:

- A hook that rewrote files would mean the commit you staged and reviewed is not the commit
  that lands.
- A *bi-directional* sync at commit time would pull another agent's edits into this project
  and broadcast them to every other tool's instruction file without review — one tool's
  change silently becoming every tool's instruction.

It only checks blocks generated from **files** (the testing matrix and the workflow). The
debt-marker block comes from a setting, which a git hook cannot read, so it is not checked
rather than guessed at.

A block that a file does not carry is never reported: adopting one tool should not become a
standing complaint about the eight you do not use.

Skip a single commit with `ATLASMIND_SKIP_INSTRUCTION_CHECK=1`. Because a git hook has no
VS Code host, this is read from `.vscode/settings.json` — so the checkbox writes **workspace**
scope, and a User-scoped value would not be seen.

enumDescriptions: Say nothing. The declared workflow is not mentioned in chat.
Follow the declared route in the same turn, without asking you to repeat the request. Default.
State what the workflow expects, then continue exactly as asked.
Refuse until you say to go ahead anyway.
atlasmind.workflow.chatGuidance.description: What AtlasMind does when a chat request would commit, push, branch, open a pull request, promote, or publish. Defaults to following the declared route in the same turn.
atlasmind.workflow.chatGuidance.markdownDescription:
What AtlasMind does when something you ask for in chat is covered by the declared workflow —
a commit, a push, a new branch, a pull request, a promotion, or a release.

- `follow` **(default)** — treats the declared workflow as a standing policy for this turn. Ask for
the outcome once; AtlasMind follows the enabled route without requiring a second "follow the
workflow" message. Existing tool approvals, automation ceilings, protected-ref checks, release
gates, and outward-write confirmations are unchanged. Unrelated working-tree edits are never
stashed or included merely to make a release clean; branch-changing delivery work should use an
isolated Git worktree when possible.
- `inform` — states what the workflow expects, then continues exactly as asked. It does not ask a
question or stop the turn.
- `gate` — refuses until you explicitly say to go ahead. Stronger, and opt-in on purpose: a prompt
that appears on every commit becomes one people learn to click through, at which point it protects
nobody and is still in the way.
- `off` — no workflow chat policy or notice.

Detection is a **published keyword table**, not a model: no model call in front of every chat turn,
and the same prompt always produces the same decision. The host passes only a narrow validated
policy object into the Orchestrator; free-form checks, blockers, and commands from the repository
never become system-prompt text.

Nothing is applied when no workflow is declared, or when the stage that owns the action is disabled.
There would be no rule to follow, and inventing one would describe a process the project never adopted.

atlasmind.website.generation.enabled.description: Allow UI Studio to generate static HTML/CSS visual guides into .atlasmind/website-preview/. Off by default.
atlasmind.website.generation.enabled.markdownDescription:
Allow the **Generate** buttons in UI Studio to call a model and write a static
HTML/CSS visual guide. For non-web profiles this is explicitly a design reference, not the
target implementation.

Off by default, and separate from `#atlasmind.website.preview.enabled#` on purpose: writing
model-authored files and opening a local port are two different decisions, and one switch
carrying both would make the second one happen without being agreed to.

Every generation shows a modal listing **each file it will write** before anything happens,
and the plan is deterministic — the same screen map and the same stage always produce the same
file list, which is what makes that dialog worth reading.

Files only ever land in `.atlasmind/website-preview/`. Your source tree is never written to;
promoting a generated design out of the preview folder is a separate, deliberate step.

atlasmind.website.preview.enabled.description: Allow AtlasMind to serve the generated UI visual guide from a local 127.0.0.1 port. Off by default.
atlasmind.website.preview.enabled.markdownDescription:
Allow UI Studio to run a small static web server so its canonical design preview can open in
VS Code's built-in browser, with a separate guarded responsive-width lab. The deterministic draft
combines saved wireframes, UI tokens, and exact Markdown content; model-generated output remains a
separate link rather than replacing that draft.

The server binds **`127.0.0.1` only** — never `0.0.0.0` — so it is not reachable from your
network. It serves nothing but `.atlasmind/website-preview/`, refuses any path that resolves
outside it, offers no directory listing, and its URL carries a random per-session token so
another process on this machine cannot simply guess the port and read your client work.

It starts only when you open a preview and stops through **Stop Preview**, when UI Studio closes,
or when the extension deactivates.

atlasmind.website.preview.port.description: Port for the local website preview server. 0 picks a free port automatically.
atlasmind.website.preview.port.markdownDescription:
The port the website preview server listens on, on `127.0.0.1`.

`0` **(default)** lets the operating system pick a free one, which is almost always what you
want — a fixed port collides with whatever else you happen to be running.

Set a specific port only if you need a stable address, for example to keep a browser tab
open across restarts. Values below 1024 are ignored and fall back to automatic.

atlasmind.website.generation.maxFiles.description: Most files a single website generation may write. A plan exceeding this is refused rather than truncated.
atlasmind.website.generation.maxFiles.markdownDescription:
The most files one **Generate** may write into `.atlasmind/website-preview/`.

A plan that exceeds the limit is **refused with the count**, never silently truncated —
a half-generated site whose missing pages look like broken links is harder to diagnose
than one that did not run.

Raise it for a large sitemap, or generate one page at a time from the wireframe canvas.

atlasmind.website.setup.enabled.description: Allow Website Studio to scaffold a project — run the framework's create command and write its config files. Off by default.
atlasmind.website.setup.enabled.markdownDescription:
Allow **Set up this stack** on the Website Studio → Stack page to run the chosen
framework's own create command and write the platform's deploy config.

Nothing runs without a modal that lists **every command with its purpose and every file with
its full contents** first. Commands are constants in AtlasMind's source — never composed from
a setting, never parsed from documentation, never written by a model — and each runs through
`execFile` with an argument array, so no shell ever sees them.

Every file and branch step is **create-only**: anything that already exists is reported
untouched rather than merged or replaced. Re-running a setup is safe.

atlasmind.website.setup.generateCi.description: Allow Website Studio to write a GitHub Actions deploy workflow into .github/workflows/. Off by default.
atlasmind.website.setup.generateCi.markdownDescription:
Include a GitHub Actions workflow when setting up a stack, implementing the
develop → staging → production deploy.

Gated separately from `#atlasmind.website.setup.enabled#` because it is the one generated
artefact that **acts on its own**: everything else AtlasMind writes sits inert until you look
at it, but a workflow runs on GitHub's infrastructure, with your repository's secrets, and it
can deploy and spend money.

The YAML comes from a declared template in AtlasMind's source with only validated values
substituted — never from a model. Production deploys declare `environment: production`, so you
can require reviewers on the GitHub side. Secrets are **named, never written**. An existing
workflow file is never overwritten.

atlasmind.website.setup.allowRemoteProje.description: Allow AtlasMind to run the hosting provider's CLI to create a remote project. Off by default; these commands authenticate as you and create billable resources.
atlasmind.website.setup.allowRemoteProje.markdownDescription:
Allow setup to actually run `wrangler pages project create`, `netlify sites:create` or
`vercel link`, instead of showing them for you to run.

Off by default, and deliberately its own switch: these commands **authenticate as you and
create real, billable resources on your account**, and a run that fails halfway leaves them
orphaned with no teardown. With this off you still get the exact command and its purpose —
you just run it yourself, which is a reasonable place to keep a decision that spends money.

enumDescriptions: npm. The default, and what every framework's documented create command assumes.
pnpm. Faster installs and a content-addressed store.
Yarn.
Bun. Fastest installs, but the youngest ecosystem support.
atlasmind.website.setup.packageManager.description: Package manager used for scaffold, dev and build commands when setting up a website stack.
atlasmind.website.setup.packageManager.markdownDescription:
Which package manager Website Studio uses in the commands it plans and in the scripts it
writes into `package.json`.

Only the leading executable and the `run`/`exec` verbs are translated; flags are passed
through untouched. That is deliberately narrow — a general translation layer would have to
understand each manager's flag differences, and getting that subtly wrong produces a command
that runs and does something other than what you read.

atlasmind.website.content.directory.description: Folder holding the Markdown screen/content files UI Studio reads and writes. Relative to the workspace root.
atlasmind.website.content.directory.markdownDescription:
Where interface copy lives, as one Markdown file per page or screen with YAML front-matter.

Files are the **source of truth**; UI Studio shows an editable mirror of them. That lets a
content designer work in their own editor, keeps copy reviewable in pull requests, and leaves
the eventual implementation free to consume or translate the content for HTML, native, or other targets.

A path that escapes the workspace is ignored and the default is used instead.

atlasmind.website.review.enabled.description: Allow Website Studio to record client review comments against pages and wireframe elements. Off by default.
atlasmind.website.review.enabled.markdownDescription:
Turn on client review: comments recorded against a page, or against a specific element on
it, tracked through `open → addressed → resolved`.

Comments **transition, never delete** — "we fixed it" and "we decided not to" are different
facts. A comment against an element somebody later removed is **kept and flagged**, because it
is the evidence that the element was removed while it was under review.

Comment text is treated as third-party input everywhere it is used, including being fenced as
reported content before it ever reaches a model.

atlasmind.website.review.includeOverlayI.description: Inject the client comment overlay into generated pages so a client can leave feedback in their own browser. Off by default.
atlasmind.website.review.includeOverlayI.markdownDescription:
Include the review overlay in generated pages, so a client can open the site and click on the
thing they want to talk about.

**AtlasMind hosts nothing.** The overlay ships inside the site itself, so it travels to the
password-protected staging environment the Stack page already sets up — your client's own
hosting. Comments come back either as a file they download and send you, or by POST to a
webhook you already own (see `#atlasmind.website.review.webhookUrl#`).

This is the **only** place AtlasMind puts JavaScript into a generated page. The overlay script
is a fixed constant in AtlasMind's source — nothing from your project is ever interpolated into
it, and its configuration travels in a data attribute instead.

atlasmind.website.review.webhookUrl.description: HTTPS endpoint the review overlay POSTs comments to. Empty means the client downloads a file instead.
atlasmind.website.review.webhookUrl.markdownDescription:
An endpoint **you already own** — a form handler, a Worker, an n8n webhook — that the review
overlay posts client comments to.

Empty (the default) means export-only: the client downloads a JSON file and sends it to you,
and you import it with **AtlasMind: Import Website Client Feedback**. No endpoint is ever
invented or defaulted, because a guessed URL would send your client's feedback to a stranger.

`https` only, and a URL carrying credentials is refused. The value is also the only origin the
generated page's content-security-policy permits a connection to.
